To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a new laser air-motion system has been developed and calibrated to measure true airspeed and that this measurement can be used to calibrate the measurements of static and dynamic pressure, which in turn can be used to measure temperature.

the new laser air motion sensor provides a basis for reducing the standard uncertainty in measurements of airspeed to 0.1m s−1, and the standard uncertainty of the measured component of relative wind along the aircraft’s longitudinal axis to 0.3 m s−1.

we have reduced uncertainty in the measurements of airspeed to less than 1% (0.1 m/s) and uncertainty in measurements of pressure to about 0% (0.3 hPa) by calibrating these measurements using a laser air-motion sensor that is independent of any other measurement.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and application of an innovative laser-based instrument to provide a measurement of the true airspeed, and the use of that measurement to calibrate the measurements of pressure and temperature, thereby reducing their uncertainty.

the development and use of an airborne system that measures true airspeed with standard uncertainty less than 0 1 m s− 1, pressure with standard uncertainty less that 0.3 Pa, and temperature with standard uncertainty less then 0.3 K.
improving the calibration of air-motion sensors and the resulting measurements of airspeed and pressure, and then using those measurements to improve the calibration of temperature sensors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this new sensor provides a means to measure airspeed and temperature that are independent of each other and of all other temperature sensors, and the measured pressures are independent of all other pressure sensors.

the new laser air motion sensor provides a means of measuring airspeed with standard uncertainty of about 0.05 m s−1, which is an order of magnitude better than the best available before, and this measurement provides a basis for improving measurements of air pressure and temperature by a factor of 2–3, and for reducing the uncertainty in these measurements by a factor of about 3.
the new laser air-speed sensor is a valuable addition to the suite of instruments used to measure the relative wind vector in the atmospheric boundary layer and the free troposphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated the capability to measure the airspeed, pressure, and temperature of an aircraft in flight, with standard uncertainties in the measurements that are significantly smaller than the uncertainties that can be achieved using standard calibration techniques.

we have developed an improved technique for measuring airspeed, pressure, temperature, and relative wind components, and we have used this technique to calibrate and validate the measurements of these quantities for one research aircraft, the National Research Council of Canada's Convair 580.

a Doppler laser sensor for measuring airspeed, combined with a pressure sensor and a global positioning system, can be used to provide an accurate and precise measurement of airspeed, static and dynamic pressure and, hence, temperature, with no dependence on the accuracy and precision of any other sensor.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the new laser sensor provides a new way of calibrating the pressure and temperature measurements of a research aircraft, which can be done in flight and so does not require the aircraft to land at a facility that can provide a calibration.

the new laser air motion sensor provides a new and improved method for calibrating pressure measurements and that these improved measurements of pressure can be used to calibrate temperature measurements.

the uncertainty in measurements of airspeed and pressure can be reduced significantly by using a laser air-motion sensor, and that this can be used to reduce the uncertainty in temperature measurements.
